newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan current account surplus falls 29% in August.
newsitem.headline: Japan current account surplus falls 29% in August.

text.p: Japan's huge surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, shrank in August as the flow of foreign goods into the country continued to strengthen.
The current account surplus in August dropped by 28.9 percent to 460.60 billion yen ($4.14 billion) from a year earlier, the Finance Ministry announced on Wednesday.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone decreased by 27.8 percent to 566.70 billion yen ($5.10 billion) from the same month a year earlier.

Economists said the drop in both figures was no surprise. Japan's current account surplus has been on a downward trend since September 1995 and August was the 21st month in a row that the merchandise trade surplus fell on a year-on-year basis.

"You've got further evidence that import growth is outpacing exports. You've got import growth almost three times as fast as Japanese export growth and that's what's reducing the overall balance," Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan in Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television.
However, economists also expected the pace of the decline in the surplus to slow because the yen 's weakness against the dollar would discourage imports.
A weak yen makes foreign products less competitive in Japanese markets because it inflates their prices in yen terms.

"Short-term, my view is that any increase in demand will be met first with domestic supply because of the yen's depreciation and therefore the rate of decline (of the surplus) will continue to narrow over the medium-term," said Merrill Lynch economist Ron Bevacqua.
"Once the yen starts to appreciate or domestic sources...reach their limit, import growth will pick up again. (But) it could be quite a while," Bevacqua said. ($1=111 yen)
